c.entradas.sello-va243.fecha_texto: Akkadian period, c. 2350–2150 BC (based on style and inscription; the exact date is approximate).
c.entradas.sello-va243.resumen: A small Akkadian cylinder seal held in the Museum of the Ancient Near East in Berlin. It shows a scene of offering or presentation before an enthroned deity. At the top is a star symbol surrounded by dots. Zecharia Sitchin presented it as a map of the solar system with an additional planet, but specialists do not accept that reading.
c.entradas.sello-va243.interpretacion:
What the seal shows: a seated figure (a god or a high-ranking person) receives other figures who present an offering. It is a very common type of scene in Akkadian and Ur III glyptic art. The inscription, in three lines of cuneiform, says nothing about astronomy. It is an ordinary ownership formula: it reads as a personal name, Dubsiga, another name, Ili-illat, and the expression 'your/his servant'. In other words, it identifies the owner of the seal as the servant of another person. The detailed reading of the names may vary among epigraphers, but its structure as an ownership formula is clear.

The 'star': the seal shows a six-pointed star surrounded by eleven dots or globes. For Assyriologists it is one of the usual astral symbols that accompany divine scenes. It does not match the typical form of the sun in Mesopotamian art, a disk with a four-pointed star and wavy rays between its points, like the emblem of Shamash. A single star with dots is usually interpreted as a star or a group of stars, and it has been proposed, for example, that the dots are simple decoration or a constellation. Moreover, Mesopotamian texts show no knowledge of the heliocentric structure of the solar system, or of Uranus, Neptune or Pluto (invisible to the naked eye). The sizes and distances of the 'planets' on the seal do not correspond to anything real. Michael Heiser and others have set out these arguments against Sitchin's reading.
c.entradas.sello-va243.detalles.0: Inventory number VA 243 of the Vorderasiatisches Museum (Pergamonmuseum), Berlin.
c.entradas.sello-va243.detalles.1: It dates to the Akkadian period, c. 2350–2150 BC.
c.entradas.sello-va243.detalles.2: The inscription is an ownership formula with two personal names (read Dubsiga and Ili-illat) and 'your servant'.
c.entradas.sello-va243.detalles.3: The symbol at the top is a six-pointed star with eleven dots around it, not the sun disk with wavy rays characteristic of Shamash.
c.entradas.sello-va243.detalles.4: Babylonian astronomy knew only five planets visible to the naked eye, plus the Sun and the Moon, and always within a geocentric model.
c.entradas.sello-va243.relaciones.utu-sh: his solar symbol differs from the seal
c.entradas.astronomia-babilonica.nombre_: Science of celestial omens (Enūma Anu Enlil) and Babylonian mathematical astronomy
c.entradas.astronomia-babilonica.fecha_t: The Venus observations of Ammi-saduqa are Old Babylonian (17th century BC, later copies). Enūma Anu Enlil and MUL.APIN date to the 2nd–1st millennia BC. The astronomical diaries run from c. 652 BC to the 1st century BC, and mathematical astronomy from c. 400 BC onward.
c.entradas.astronomia-babilonica.resumen: The Babylonians observed the sky for centuries, mainly to interpret omens. Over time they created precise mathematical methods to predict the movements of the Moon and the planets. It is one of the oldest scientific traditions in the world and the basis of Greek astronomy.
c.entradas.astronomia-babilonica.interpr:
The original motivation was divination: the sky was seen as a 'writing' of the gods. The omen series Enūma Anu Enlil, of some 70 tablets, collects thousands of omens. The scholars who advised the Assyrian kings, whose letters are preserved at Nineveh, interpreted eclipses and planetary appearances for the king.

From the 5th century BC, the astronomers of Babylon and Uruk developed arithmetical models (the 'Systems A and B') to predict lunar and planetary phenomena. They introduced the zodiac of twelve signs of 30 degrees. Mathieu Ossendrijver (Science, 2016) showed that they also used geometrical methods, calculating Jupiter's displacement as the area of a trapezoid. Their whole system is geocentric and limited to the bodies visible to the naked eye: the Sun, the Moon and five planets.
c.entradas.astronomia-babilonica.detalle: The astronomical diaries record observations almost without interruption from c. 652 BC to the 1st century BC.
The Venus tablet of Ammi-saduqa (Enūma Anu Enlil, Tablet 63) is key to the debate on chronology.
The zodiac of twelve signs of 30 degrees is a Babylonian creation (c. 5th century BC).
Ossendrijver (2016) published five tablets, from c. 350–50 BC, with geometrical calculations of Jupiter.
Hipparchus and Ptolemy used Babylonian eclipse observations and parameters.
c.entradas.astronomia-babilonica.fuentes: Mathematical astronomy texts from Babylon and Uruk
c.entradas.biblioteca-asurbanipal.nombre: Tablet collections of the palaces and temples of Nineveh (7th century BC)
c.entradas.biblioteca-asurbanipal.fecha_: Assembled mainly under Ashurbanipal (668–c. 631 BC). Nineveh was destroyed in 612 BC and has been excavated since 1849–1854 (Layard, Rassam).
c.entradas.biblioteca-asurbanipal.resume: A large collection of cuneiform tablets assembled at Nineveh by the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal. It preserved copies of much of Mesopotamian literature, religion and science, including Gilgamesh and the Enuma Elish.
c.entradas.biblioteca-asurbanipal.interp:
Ashurbanipal, who boasted that he could read and write, had tablets copied and requisitioned in Babylonia to gather the knowledge needed to rule: omens, incantations, rituals, lexical lists and literature. Most are texts for practical use and divination, not 'literature' in the modern sense.

The burning of Nineveh in 612 BC baked many tablets and helped preserve them. Today the British Museum holds more than 30,000 tablets and fragments from Kuyunjik (Nineveh).
c.entradas.biblioteca-asurbanipal.detall: There are more than 30,000 tablets and fragments in the British Museum.
It was excavated by Austen Henry Layard and Hormuzd Rassam in the mid-19th century.
The Gilgamesh flood tablet (K 3375), identified by George Smith in 1872, was found there.
Many tablets bear colophons with Ashurbanipal's name.
c.entradas.biblioteca-asurbanipal.fuente: Kuyunjik (Nineveh), K collection of the British Museum
c.entradas.akitu.fecha_texto: Attested from the 3rd millennium BC at Ur and Nippur. The Babylonian version for Marduk is documented mainly in the 1st millennium BC, through Seleucid-period rituals.
c.entradas.akitu.resumen: The great religious New Year festival, held in Babylon during the first twelve days of the month of Nisannu, in spring. During it the Enuma Elish was recited, the king renewed his legitimacy before Marduk, and the god's statue went out in procession.
c.entradas.akitu.interpretacion:
Religion and politics came together in the festival. During the ritual, the high priest took away the king's insignia and slapped him; the king declared that he had not sinned and got his insignia back. If he wept, it was a good omen. The king's presence was essential: when Nabonidus was away at Tayma, the festival was not held, and the chronicles criticize him for it.

The recitation of the Enuma Elish on the fourth day is known from late rituals. Early 20th-century theories that reconstructed the festival as a drama of Marduk's 'death and resurrection' were based on misreadings and have now been discarded.
c.entradas.akitu.detalles.0: It lasted twelve days, in the month of Nisannu (March–April).
c.entradas.akitu.detalles.1: The Enuma Elish was recited on the fourth day.
c.entradas.akitu.detalles.2: The ritual humiliation of the king took place on the fifth day.
c.entradas.akitu.detalles.3: Marduk's statue went out through the Ishtar Gate toward the 'akitu house', outside the city.
c.entradas.akitu.fuentes_primarias.0: Seleucid ritual texts from Babylon (Louvre, British Museum)
c.entradas.tablilla-perdida-enlil.nombre: There is no ancient original form. "Lost Tablet of Enlil" is a modern, popular name, spread mainly through YouTube videos from 2025; it does not appear in museum catalogs or in the ETCSL, ORACC or CDLI corpora. The closest ancient object is the "Tablet of Destinies" (Akkadian ṭuppi šīmāti; Sumerian dub nam-tar-ra), which Enlil keeps in the myths.
c.entradas.tablilla-perdida-enlil.fecha_: There is no ancient text with this name. The materials the title draws on are: tablet Ni 12501 (Early Dynastic IIIb, c. 2400 BC), Atrahasis (Old Babylonian, c. 1700–1640 BC) and the myth of Anzu (Old Babylonian and Standard versions of the 1st millennium BC).
c.entradas.tablilla-perdida-enlil.resume: The "Lost Tablet of Enlil" is not an identified ancient object or text: there is no tablet by that name in museums or in academic editions. It is a sensationalist title from alternative popular-history videos circulating since 2025. They mix the real news about tablet Ni 12501 (a "forgotten" Sumerian myth in which Enlil summons the gods) with the story of Atrahasis, in which Enlil decides to wipe out humankind, and with Zecharia Sitchin's reading of the Anunnaki.
c.entradas.tablilla-perdida-enlil.interp:
In Assyriology there is no "Lost Tablet of Enlil". Most likely the name is a popular hook formed from several real elements. (1) In July and August 2025 the press reported on the work of Jana Matuszak (University of Chicago) in the journal Iraq: the first complete edition of Ni 12501, a fragmentary tablet from Nippur (c. 2400 BC) held in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums. Samuel Noah Kramer had reproduced it on the dust jacket of his 1956 book and described it as "another Enlil myth, still unpublished". In it the storm god Iškur is trapped in the Kur (the Underworld), which causes a drought; Enlil gathers the gods to find someone to rescue him, and only a fox volunteers. The headlines spoke of a "lost" or "forgotten" myth. (2) At the same time, videos appeared with titles such as "The Lost Tablet of Enlil Finally Recovered — It Describes His Vote Against Humanity" and "The Lost Tablet of Enlil Finally Translated — It Describes Why He Wanted Humans Destroyed". Their storyline, that Enlil voted in the divine assembly to destroy humankind, does not come from Ni 12501. It is the story of Atrahasis and of Tablet XI of Gilgamesh, which have been known and published since the 19th century.

A third source of the name is the Tablet of Destinies, the only mythical object explicitly associated with Enlil that is actually "lost" in a story. In the myth of Anzu, the bird Anzu steals it from Enlil while he is bathing, and Ninurta recovers it. In the Enuma Elish, Qingu holds it and Marduk takes it from him. Nor should the title be confused with real texts that have Enlil in their name, such as "Enlil in the Ekur" (ETCSL 4.05.1), "Enlil and Ninlil" (ETCSL 1.2.1), "Enlil and Sud" (ETCSL 1.2.2) or the astrological series Enuma Anu Enlil, or with Sitchin's "The Lost Book of Enki" (2002), whose formula the title copies. There is also a novel with a similar title, "The Book of Enlil" by Stephen C. Norton, an alternate-history fiction about some forgotten tablets in the British Museum.
c.entradas.tablilla-perdida-enlil.detall: In the CDLI, the ETCSL, the ORACC and the collections of the British Museum and the Penn Museum there is no text or object called the "Lost Tablet of Enlil".

Ni 12501 (CDLI P221771) is an Early Dynastic IIIb tablet (c. 2400 BC) from Nippur, held in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums. It was edited by J. Matuszak in Iraq 86 (2024), pp. 79–108, doi:10.1017/irq.2024.19. About a third of the text survives.

Kramer used Ni 12501 on the dust jacket of "From the Tablets of Sumer" (1956) with the caption "another Enlil myth, still unpublished". This is the most direct documented connection between an "unpublished" or "lost" tablet and Enlil.

In Atrahasis (Old Babylonian, c. 1700–1640 BC), Enlil, annoyed by the noise of humans, sends them plagues and then the flood. Enki/Ea thwarts him by warning Atrahasis. This is the content that the 2025 videos attribute to the supposed "lost tablet".
The Tablet of Destinies (ṭuppi šīmāti) appears in the myth of Anzu as a possession of Enlil that Anzu steals and Ninurta recovers. In the Enuma Elish it passes from Qingu to Marduk.

The videos that popularized the title in 2025 come from channels such as "The Lost Vault" and "The Obsidian Vault". Their titles use the "Finally Recovered/Translated" format typical of sensationalist popularization.
c.entradas.tablilla-perdida-enlil.fuente: Ni 12501 (Istanbul Archaeology Museums; CDLI P221771): Sumerian myth of Iškur held captive in the Kur and the assembly summoned by Enlil
Atrahasis (Old Babylonian version from Nippur/Sippar; ed. Lambert and Millard 1969)
Myth of Anzu (Old Babylonian and Standard versions; theft of Enlil's Tablet of Destinies)
Enuma Elish, Tablets I, IV and V (Qingu's Tablet of Destinies passes to Marduk)
Enlil in the Ekur (ETCSL 4.05.1); Enlil and Ninlil (ETCSL 1.2.1); Enlil and Sud (ETCSL 1.2.2); The Cursing of Agade (ETCSL 2.1.5)
Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet XI (Standard version): the flood decided by Enlil
